newsitem.title: USA: SWIMMING-GROTE EYES 2000 GAMES AFTER YEAR'S BEST BREASTSTROKE.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-GROTE EYES 2000 GAMES AFTER YEAR'S BEST BREASTSTROKE.

text.p: Kurt Grote recorded the world's fastest 200-meter breaststroke of the year at the U.S. Swimming Nationals Wednesday, then became the first U.S. Olympian to declare he will go for gold at the 2000 Games in Sydney.
The 23-year-old Grote completed a sweep of the meet's two breaststroke events Wednesday night with a career-best of two minutes 12.35 seconds in the 200 meters.

Grote, who won the 100 breaststroke earlier this week, dropped nearly four seconds off his morning qualifying time in the 200 final for the third fastest time by an American in the event and eighth fastest ever in the world.
"I don't think I sped up, I think everyone else just slowed down," said Grote, whose previous best time in the 200 breaststroke was 2:13.96 at the 1996 Olympic Trials.
"Hopefully, I have a lot more career-bests in me."
The seven-day meet is serving as U.S. selection trials for the FINA World Championships in Perth, Australia, the Pan Pacific Championships in Fukuoka, Japan, and the World University Games in Sicily.
In other finals Wednesday, Olympian Kristine Quance won the 200-meter individual medley in a lifetime best 2:13.55.
She has now qualified for the world championships in the 200 and 400 IM and 100-meter breaststroke.
Neil Walker, after breaking his left hand at the collegiate national championships in March, won the 100-meter butterfly in a career-best 53.06.
Grote won a gold medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games as a member of the 400-meter medley relay team, but failed to medal in his individual events.
For that reason the second-year Stanford medical student is already talking about making the 2000 Olympic team.
"There were mixed emotions after the Olympics," Grote said.
"I didn't tap my potential in either of my events," explained Grote, who finished sixth in the 100 and eighth in the 200 in Atlanta.
Grote said he will take a year off from med school in 1999 to train for the Olympic trials.
"I knew as soon as the last Olympics were over, I needed to keep trying and go for an individual medal," he said. "That's where my heart is."
